pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.1: The numbering begins with five because the first four rules have been omitted. This is because these rules are almost identical to the rules entailing expulsion for the monks, the only difference being the first rule, which is worded slightly differently.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.12: “Nunnery” renders upassaya. According to the word definition at Bu Pc 23, this includes any place where a nun stays. In other words, it spans anything from a single hut, see Bi Pc 35, to a monastery. The Jain text The Ācārāṅga-sūtra, contains a passage that describes an upassaya as including a grassy area, that is, it must have been a compound of buildings or a monastery: “A layman might, for the sake of a mendicant … cutting and clipping the grass outside or within the upāśraya (= upassaya).” See Jacobi, Hermann, trans. “Jaina Sutras Part I”. Motilal Babarsidass, 1964, p. 94.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.22: For a discussion of the rendering “gatehouse” for koṭṭhaka, see Appendix of Technical Terms.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.32: “Intimate with” renders dūsetuṁ. For a discussion of the meaning of dūseti, see Appendix of Technical Terms.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.52: “Training” renders vinaya. For a discussion of this word, see Appendix of Technical Terms.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:1.54.1: For a detailed discussion of this rule, see Appendix on Individual Bhikkhunī Rules.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:2.2.2: Something connected to the body means any contact that is not skin to skin, such as contact through clothes. That touching through clothes does not count as touching body to body is supported by two of the Vinayas in Chinese translation, namely, the Dharmaguptaska Vinaya and the Sarvāstivāda Vinaya.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:2.2.15.1: The Pali just says that, “One of them has lust”, ekatoavassute, without specifying who. However, it seems reasonable that this should refer to the nun, since it is hard to imagine she would incur an offense if her mind were pure. This supposition is supported by Sp 2.662: Ekatoavassuteti ettha kiñcāpi ekatoti avisesena vuttaṁ, tathāpi bhikkhuniyā eva avassute sati ayaṁ āpattibhedo vuttoti veditabbo, “‘One of them has lust’: here, although it is said ‘one of them’ without distinction, still it is to be understood that this offense is said to be incurred only when the nun has lust.”
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:2.2.29.1: In this case, it seems implied by the genitive case ending for the various kinds of beings that it is only the nun who is making the contact. This is unexpected, since in the main rule the nun is not doing the touching, but is instead being touched. It is possible that the text here has been corrupted. For a detailed discussion of this case, see Appendix on Individual Bhikkhunī Rules. | All the beings here must be male. This is implied by the fact that there is no offense for touching or being touched by a human female. | For a discussion of paṇḍaka, see Appendix of Technical Terms.
pli-tv-bi-vb-pj5:2.3.10: The Pali says the “first offense”, but since I am including the four rules entailing expulsion that the nuns have in common with the monks, I get “fifth offense” instead. That this is the correct way of counting is confirmed by the word-commentary of the present rule, which states that the pi, “too”, of ayampi refers to the preceding pārājika rules. The equivalent adjustment is required for the next three rules entailing expulsion.
